newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Grain barons to win in EU farm price marathon.
newsitem.headline: Grain barons to win in EU farm price marathon.

text.p: Plans to slash aid to wealthy wheat farmers are likely to be pushed aside at an annual European Union farm price marathon starting in Luxembourg on Monday, EU diplomats said.

Farm ministers, except Britain's and Sweden's, are expected to block EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fishler's bid to cut payments to cereals and oilseed farmers by 1.4 billion ecus ($1.6 billion) to help finance aid for beef producers crippled by the mad cow crisis.

The cereals aid cut is the most contentious issue in a package of farm prices and measures for the coming 12 months which, if an EU ritual is respected, will be thrashed out after an all-night session after several days of hard bargaining.

Germany, France and other countries argue that it is unfair to make cereals farmers foot the bill for damage caused by bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) and that there are sufficient savings in the farm budget to cover the cost.
"It's hard to see how Fischler can succeed," said a diplomat, noting that a similar plan was thrown out last year.
But the EU's burly Austrian farm chief, armed with studies showing cereals farmers have been grossly overpaid, is unwilling to budge.

The Commission's agriculture directorate has estimated that cereals farmers were overpaid by 8.5 billion ecus ($9.6 billion) during the past four marketing years. A British study put the excess much higher at 14.3 billion ecus ($16.2 billion).
The payments were intended to compensate farmers for cuts in support prices agreed under 1992 farm reforms to remove grain, beef and dairy surpluses and to curb costs.
Since then cereals market prices have soared but farmers have still been paid for losses they never suffered.
"It's difficult for finance ministers to tolerate, harder still for taxpayers," said a sceptical official.

Over 40 percent of the 41 billion ecus ($46 billion) EU farm budget is spent on cereals but the funds go mostly to a minority of large, wealthy farmers -- the so-called grain barons of northern France and Germany and eastern England.
But ministers, who need Fischler's support for long shopping lists of sweeteners to a bland package of mainly unchanged farm prices, are expected to find a face-saving formula.
France's new farm minister Louis Le Pensec, who met Fischler on Friday, suggested that the proposal could be reviewed as part of future farm reforms.
"It would keep the idea alive," said an official.
Top of France's and most other shopping lists is an urgent demand to fix how much cereals land farmers must take out of production in 1998 in order to benefit from EU subsidies.

In the absence of a proposal from Fischler, they are expected next week to urge him to recommend an unchanged set- aside rate of five percent. It would represent a compromise between French demands for as low a rate as possible, ideally zero, and Germany's preference for 10 percent or more.
Ministers will also seek weaker penalties for overplanting cereals, increases in milk quotas and extra aid for sheep, tobacco, olive oil and peas and beans farmers.
The Dutch EU Presidency is confident that a deal will be struck next week but once again it is likely to be announced by bleary-eyed officials after an exhausting all-night session.
